title: Learn Linux
summary: A complete learning path from your first command to Linux administration: shell skills, security, services, networking, storage, automation and incident recovery. Practice in TuxOS, then complete the companion labs on a disposable Ubuntu/Debian VM.

lessons.title: First words with the shell
lessons.story: A terminal is a conversation: you type a command, press Enter, and the computer answers. Let's ask it three simple questions.

steps.task: Ask the computer who you are: type whoami and press Enter.
hints: Open the Terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T), type whoami and press Enter.
steps.explain: whoami prints the user you are logged in as. Everything you do runs as that user.
steps.teach: whoami prints the user you are logged in as. Everything you do runs as that user. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Open the Terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T), type whoami and press Enter.

hints: pwd stands for print working directory. Type pwd and press Enter.
steps.explain: You start in your home folder, /home/<you>. The prompt shows it as ~.
steps.teach: You start in your home folder, /home/<you>. The prompt shows it as ~. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. pwd stands for print working directory. Type pwd and press Enter.

hints: ls lists what is in the current folder. Type ls and press Enter.
steps.explain: ls is the command you will type most often. Folders and files are listed by name.
steps.teach: ls is the command you will type most often. Folders and files are listed by name. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. ls lists what is in the current folder. Type ls and press Enter.

outcomes: First words with the shell
lessons.realLab: Repeat this lesson in a disposable Ubuntu VM under your own non-root account. Compare help output and note any differences from TuxOS. Use a practice directory and inspect paths before changing files.

lessons.title: Moving around
lessons.story: Someone left a garden in your home folder, and something is hidden in it. Folders are called directories, and cd (change directory) moves you between them.

files.~/garden/.seed-packet: The hidden seed is a sunflower.

steps.task: Go into the garden directory: cd garden
hints: From your home folder, type cd garden. Watch the prompt change to ~/garden.
steps.explain: The prompt always shows where you are. cd with no arguments takes you back home.
steps.teach: The prompt always shows where you are. cd with no arguments takes you back home. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. From your home folder, type cd garden. Watch the prompt change to ~/garden.

steps.task: Some files are hidden. Show everything with ls -a
hints: Names starting with a dot are hidden from plain ls.
Type ls -a inside the garden.
steps.explain: -a means all. Files whose names start with a dot are hidden by convention, often settings.
steps.teach: -a means all. Files whose names start with a dot are hidden by convention, often settings. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Names starting with a dot are hidden from plain ls.

steps.task: Read the hidden file with cat to find out what the seed is.
hints: cat prints a file. The file is called .seed-packet (with the dot).
Type cat .seed-packet
steps.explain: cat (from concatenate) prints files. Tab completes names, so cat .se then Tab saves typing.
steps.teach: cat (from concatenate) prints files. Tab completes names, so cat .se then Tab saves typing. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. cat prints a file. The file is called .seed-packet (with the dot).

steps.task: Go back up to your home folder with cd ..
hints: .. means the folder above this one. Type cd ..
steps.explain: .. is the parent folder and . is the current one. They work in every path, like ../garden/shed.
steps.teach: .. is the parent folder and . is the current one. They work in every path, like ../garden/shed. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. .. means the folder above this one. Type cd ..

outcomes: Moving around

lessons.title: Making, copying and removing
lessons.story: Time to build your own corner of the system: a project folder with a plan in it.

steps.task: Make a directory called projects: mkdir projects
hints: mkdir means make directory. Type mkdir projects in your home folder.
steps.explain: mkdir -p makes a whole path at once, like mkdir -p a/b/c.
steps.teach: mkdir -p makes a whole path at once, like mkdir -p a/b/c. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. mkdir means make directory. Type mkdir projects in your home folder.

steps.task: Write the words learn linux into projects/plan.txt using echo and >
hints: > sends a command's output into a file instead of the screen.
Type echo learn linux > projects/plan.txt
steps.explain: > replaces a file's contents and >> adds to the end. Careful: > overwrites without asking.
steps.teach: > replaces a file's contents and >> adds to the end. Careful: > overwrites without asking. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. > sends a command's output into a file instead of the screen.

steps.task: Make a backup: copy plan.txt to plan.bak in the same folder.
hints: cp takes a source and a destination.
Type cp projects/plan.txt projects/plan.bak
steps.explain: cp copies, mv moves or renames, and both take the source first and the destination second.
steps.teach: cp copies, mv moves or renames, and both take the source first and the destination second. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. cp takes a source and a destination.

steps.task: Open the Files app from the desktop and look inside projects.
hints: Double-click the Files icon on the desktop, then double-click projects.
steps.explain: Files and the terminal show the same filesystem. Change something in one and the other sees it.
steps.teach: Files and the terminal show the same filesystem. Change something in one and the other sees it. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Double-click the Files icon on the desktop, then double-click projects.

steps.task: You don't need the backup after all. Delete projects/plan.bak with rm.
hints: rm removes files. There is no recycle bin in the terminal.
Type rm projects/plan.bak
steps.explain: rm deletes for good. rm -r removes a folder and everything in it, so read twice before pressing Enter.
steps.teach: rm deletes for good. rm -r removes a folder and everything in it, so read twice before pressing Enter. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. rm removes files. There is no recycle bin in the terminal.

outcomes: Making, copying and removing

lessons.title: Reading and searching
lessons.story: A web server has been writing a log all night. Logs are long, so instead of reading everything you'll ask questions about it.

files.~/logs/server.log:
08:00 INFO server started
08:01 INFO request /home
08:02 ERROR database timeout
08:03 INFO request /about
08:04 WARN slow response
08:05 ERROR disk almost full
08:06 INFO request /home
08:07 ERROR database timeout
08:08 INFO request /contact
08:09 INFO server healthy

steps.task: Show only the first 3 lines of logs/server.log with head.
hints: head shows the start of a file. -n chooses how many lines.
Type head -n 3 logs/server.log
steps.explain: tail shows the end instead, which is where the newest log lines are.
steps.teach: tail shows the end instead, which is where the newest log lines are. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. head shows the start of a file. -n chooses how many lines.

steps.task: How many lines does the log have? Count them with wc -l
hints: wc counts lines, words and characters; -l means just lines.
Type wc -l logs/server.log
steps.explain: 10 lines. On a real server, logs can have millions, which is why these tools matter.
steps.teach: 10 lines. On a real server, logs can have millions, which is why these tools matter. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. wc counts lines, words and characters; -l means just lines.

steps.task: Show only the ERROR lines with grep.
hints: grep prints the lines that contain a pattern.
Type grep ERROR logs/server.log
steps.explain: grep is one of the most useful commands there is. grep -i ignores case and grep -r searches folders.
steps.teach: grep is one of the most useful commands there is. grep -i ignores case and grep -r searches folders. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. grep prints the lines that contain a pattern.

steps.task: Now just count the errors with grep -c
hints: -c makes grep print how many lines matched instead of the lines.
Type grep -c ERROR logs/server.log
steps.explain: Three errors. Small questions with exact answers are how you find problems quickly.
steps.teach: Three errors. Small questions with exact answers are how you find problems quickly. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. -c makes grep print how many lines matched instead of the lines.

outcomes: Reading and searching

lessons.title: Pipes: chaining commands
lessons.story: The real power of the shell is joining small commands together. A pipe | sends one command's output into the next.

files.~/fruit.txt:
banana
apple
cherry
apple
banana
apple

hints: Type sort fruit.txt
steps.explain: sort puts lines in order. sort -r reverses it and sort -n sorts numbers properly.
steps.teach: sort puts lines in order. sort -r reverses it and sort -n sorts numbers properly. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Type sort fruit.txt

steps.task: Count how many of each fruit there are by piping sort into uniq -c
hints: uniq only merges repeated lines that are next to each other, so sort first.
Type sort fruit.txt | uniq -c
steps.explain: sort | uniq -c is a classic: it turns a list into a tally. Add | sort -rn to rank it.
steps.teach: sort | uniq -c is a classic: it turns a list into a tally. Add | sort -rn to rank it. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. uniq only merges repeated lines that are next to each other, so sort first.

steps.task: Save the sorted fruit into sorted.txt using >
hints: Redirection works after any command, including a pipeline.
Type sort fruit.txt > sorted.txt
steps.explain: Commands, pipes and redirection together are how people automate work on Linux.
steps.teach: Commands, pipes and redirection together are how people automate work on Linux. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Redirection works after any command, including a pipeline.

outcomes: Pipes: chaining commands

lessons.title: Permissions and sudo
lessons.story: Linux decides who may read, change or run every file. You'll meet a file you can't read, borrow root's power, and protect a file of your own.

files.~/diary.txt: Today I learned that ls -l shows permissions.

steps.task: See the permissions of your files with ls -l
hints: Type ls -l. The first column, like -rw-r--r--, is the permissions.
steps.explain: rw-r--r-- means: you (owner) can read and write, your group and everyone else can only read.
steps.teach: rw-r--r-- means: you (owner) can read and write, your group and everyone else can only read. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Type ls -l. The first column, like -rw-r--r--, is the permissions.

steps.task: Try to read the password file: cat /etc/shadow
hints: Type cat /etc/shadow. It's supposed to fail!
steps.explain: /etc/shadow holds password hashes, so only root, the administrator, may read it.
steps.teach: /etc/shadow holds password hashes, so only root, the administrator, may read it. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Type cat /etc/shadow. It's supposed to fail!

steps.task: Run the same command as root by putting sudo in front of it.
hints: sudo means do this as the superuser.
Type sudo cat /etc/shadow
steps.explain: sudo is powerful: root can change or delete anything. Use it only when you understand the command.
steps.teach: sudo is powerful: root can change or delete anything. Use it only when you understand the command. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. sudo means do this as the superuser.

steps.task: Make your diary private: only you may read or write it. Use chmod 600 diary.txt
hints: 600 means read+write (6) for you, nothing (0) for group, nothing (0) for others.
Type chmod 600 diary.txt, then ls -l to check.
steps.explain: Each digit adds read (4), write (2) and execute (1). 644 is a typical file and 755 a typical program.
steps.teach: Each digit adds read (4), write (2) and execute (1). 644 is a typical file and 755 a typical program. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. 600 means read+write (6) for you, nothing (0) for group, nothing (0) for others.

outcomes: Permissions and sudo

lessons.title: Installing software with apt
lessons.story: Linux installs programs from package repositories with a package manager. On Ubuntu that is apt. You'll find out why apt needs root, refresh its package lists, and install a program called tree.

steps.task: Try to install the tree program without sudo: apt install tree
hints: Type apt install tree. It's supposed to fail!
steps.explain: Installing software changes the whole system, so apt only lets root do it.
steps.teach: Installing software changes the whole system, so apt only lets root do it. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Type apt install tree. It's supposed to fail!

steps.task: Refresh the list of available packages as root: sudo apt update
hints: apt update downloads the latest list of packages. It needs root too.
Type sudo apt update
steps.explain: apt update refreshes the package lists. Do it before installing, or apt may not find the package.
steps.teach: apt update refreshes the package lists. Do it before installing, or apt may not find the package. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. apt update downloads the latest list of packages. It needs root too.

steps.task: Install tree as root: sudo apt install tree
hints: Put sudo in front: sudo apt install tree
steps.explain: apt downloaded the package, unpacked it, and put the tree program in /usr/bin.
steps.teach: apt downloaded the package, unpacked it, and put the tree program in /usr/bin. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Put sudo in front: sudo apt install tree

hints: Just type tree and press Enter.
steps.explain: tree draws your folders as a tree. sudo apt remove uninstalls a package, and apt list --installed shows what you have.
steps.teach: tree draws your folders as a tree. sudo apt remove uninstalls a package, and apt list --installed shows what you have. Read the task, inspect the command and its arguments, then run it yourself. Just type tree and press Enter.

outcomes: Installing software with apt

hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: cd ~
steps.explain: ~ expands to your home. cd with no argument also returns home.

steps.teach: mkdir -p creates missing parent directories and succeeds when a directory already exists.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: mkdir -p ~/admin-practice/reports

lessons.title: Quoting, wildcards and safe filenames
lessons.story: A report directory contains names with spaces. Select exactly the files you mean before copying or deleting.
outcomes: Quoting, wildcards and safe filenames
Verify the result before moving on

steps.task: Read the file whose name contains a space.
steps.teach: Quote the part of a path that contains spaces: ~/quoting/"month report.txt". Leave ~ unquoted so the shell expands it to your home directory. Quotes keep the filename in one argument.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: cat ~/quoting/"month report.txt"
steps.explain: In TuxOS, a leading ~ is expanded during path resolution even inside quotes; in Bash use "$HOME/quoting/month report.txt" or quote only the space-containing part. Quotes keep spaces in one argument.

steps.teach: The shell expands * to matching filenames. Check the expansion with ls before using a destructive command.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: ls ~/quoting/*.log
steps.explain: The shell expands * to matching filenames. Check the expansion with ls before using a destructive command.

steps.task: Write a literal dollar sign to a note.
steps.teach: Single quotes preserve literal characters such as $. Double quotes preserve spaces but still allow variable expansion.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: echo 'Cost: $5' > ~/quoting/cost.txt
steps.explain: Single quotes preserve literal characters such as $. Double quotes preserve spaces but still allow variable expansion.

steps.task: Rename the report to a name without spaces.
steps.teach: mv takes a source and destination. Quoting the source keeps it one filename.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: mv ~/quoting/"month report.txt" ~/quoting/month-report.txt
steps.explain: mv takes a source and destination. Quoting the source keeps it one filename.

lessons.title: Environment variables and exit status

steps.task: Set the ROLE environment variable to operator.
steps.teach: export NAME=value sets a shell variable for subsequent commands. Do not put spaces around =.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: export ROLE=operator
steps.explain: export NAME=value sets a shell variable for subsequent commands. Do not put spaces around =.

steps.teach: Double quotes allow $ROLE to expand while keeping the result one argument.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: echo "$ROLE"
steps.explain: Double quotes allow $ROLE to expand while keeping the result one argument.

steps.teach: env lists environment variables. Pipes pass text from stdout into the next command.
hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: env | grep ROLE
steps.explain: env lists environment variables. Pipes pass text from stdout into the next command.

steps.task: Run false to produce a failure exit status.

hints: Use the syntax from the explanation, and check the target path or unit.
Try: false

steps.task: Print the previous exit status immediately.

Try: echo $?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
service="${1:-nginx}"
if systemctl is-active --quiet "$service"; then
